title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
A fabricated news article circulated online featuring a fake interview between a real finance presenter and a real central bank official discussing an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The interview never occurred. This represents deployment of AI-generated content as an impersonation tool, integrated into a broader scam infrastructure that included fake websites and testimonials designed to appear credible to potential investors.

The failure was in the distribution and circulation of synthetic media without verification. No human editorial check appears to have caught that the interview was fabricated before it spread. The scam exploited the difficulty audiences face in distinguishing AI-generated text and deepfake content from authentic journalism, especially when presented alongside corroborating false websites and testimonials that reinforce the deception.

It is not established whether the specific AI systems used to generate the content were developed or trained with the intent to facilitate fraud, or whether they included safeguards against misuse that the scammers circumvented.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake article circulated online featuring a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock. The article, which has since been removed, depicted an increasingly heated exchange about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never actually occurred, representing a growing trend of AI-generated investment scams that ASIC, Australia's financial regulator, says are becoming more sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC's recent research reveals that scams using deepfake content have increased dramatically, with the regulator taking down 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent and fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and wealthy individuals including Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. Rather than using isolated fake videos, scammers now create elaborate webs of deception with fake news articles, websites, and testimonials. ASIC recommends consumers verify financial service licenses through its public registers before investing and remain cautious despite polished online content.
